**“Why 202 and a status endpoint?”** Long work shouldn’t block the request; 202 means accepted for processing. **“What if the worker crashes mid-task?”** With acks_late the message is redelivered; idempotent design (deterministic ids, replace-notappend) makes redelivery safe. **“How do you choose chunk size?”** Start around 300 to 400 tokens with ~10-15% overlap, stay under the embedder’s limit, then _measure_ recall@k across sizes (you’ll do this in M8) instead of copying a default. **“What’s the hardest part of RAG in practice?”** Ingestion quality: parsing and chunking.

**Goal:** after chunking, each chunk is embedded twice (a **dense** meaning vector and a **sparse** BM25 keyword vector) and stored in one Qdrant collection with a tenant-safe payload. Documents reach ready . Deleting a document removes its vectors. You can inspect the data. 

**Time:** about 5 hours.

**Embeddings.** An embedding model turns text into a list of numbers (a **vector** ) so that texts with similar _meaning_ land close together, even with zero shared words: “can I get my money back?” sits near “refunds are processed within 30 days”. bge-base-env1.5 outputs **768 numbers** per text. Facts to know cold: 

- **Bi-encoder:** query and chunk are embedded _separately_ ; chunk vectors are computed once at ingestion, so search is fast. **Max sequence length: 512 tokens.** Longer input is truncated. 

- **Normalization:** with unit-length vectors, cosine similarity equals dot product. Use normalize_embeddings=True and the cosine distance in Qdrant. 

- **Query vs document:** BGE’s model card recommends prefixing _short queries_ (not documents) with "Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: " for retrieval. For v1.5 it’s optional and its benefit is small, so treat it as a **hyperparameter you A/B in M8** , not a religion. 

- **A model defines its own coordinate system.** Vectors from different models are not comparable. This is why the model name goes into the collection name.

**Safe file handling.** Never trust filename or Content-Type . Check size limits, detect the real type from the file’s first bytes (“magic bytes”), generate your own storage name (never use the client’s path), and compute a **SHA-256 content hash** . The hash gives free deduplication: same tenant + same hash returns the existing document instead of reprocessing (an idempotent upload).

**Parsing: turning a file into clean, ordered text.** Real documents are hostile: multi-column PDFs interleave columns if extracted naively; tables become number soup; scanned PDFs contain _no text at all_ ; HTML is 80% navigation and ads. Poor parsing poisons everything downstream, and it is the most common real cause of “my RAG is bad”. Your toolkit: pymupdf4llm (PDF to Markdown, preserving headings and tables; note PyMuPDF is AGPL-licensed, fine for a portfolio project but know it), trafilatura (main content out of HTML), plain reading for .md / .txt . Converting everything to **Markdown** gives you a structure (headings) that chunking can exploit. If a PDF yields almost no text, mark it failed with “no extractable text (needs OCR)” instead of silently indexing nothing.

**Chunking: why, and the trade-off.** You can’t embed a whole document: the embedding model has a token limit ( **bge-base: 512 tokens; longer input is silently truncated** ), and one vector per document would blur many topics together. You also can’t paste whole documents into every prompt (cost, and models get worse with noise). So you split into **chunks** , and chunk size is a fundamental trade-off: 

**Small chunks** : precise matches, cheap prompts, but may lack the context needed to answer. 

**Large chunks** : more context, but the vector “averages” several ideas, so matching is blurrier and prompts cost more.

**Why evaluate.** Without a metric, “it works well” is an opinion and every change is a guess. With one, RAG tuning becomes engineering: change one thing, re-run, compare. Evaluation has two layers. **Retrieval evaluation** asks “did the right evidence come back?” (cheap, deterministic, no LLM). **Generation evaluation** asks “given the evidence, was the answer faithful, relevant and correct?” (needs a judge). Always evaluate retrieval first: a wrong answer is usually a retrieval failure in disguise.

**Building the eval set.** Aim for 50 to 60 questions over a corpus you understand (15 to 25 documents: for instance the Markdown docs of an open-source project you know well, plus 3 or 4 PDFs for parsing variety). Mix types deliberately: 

|**Type**|**Share**|**Tests**|
|---|---|---|
|Factoid (answer in one chunk)|~35%|basic recall|
|Paraphrase (no keyword overlap)|~20%|dense strength|
|Exact-token (codes, names, flags)|~15%|sparse strength|
|Multi-chunk / comparison|~15%|context assembly|
|**Unanswerable**|~15%|refusal behavior, hallucination|

|Multi-chunk / comparison|~15%|context assembly|
|**Unanswerable**|~15%|refusal behavior, hallucination|
**Label evidence, not chunk ids.** Chunk ids change whenever you change chunking, which would invalidate your labels in the very experiments you want to run. Instead label each question with the **document and a short verbatim text span** that contains the answer. A retrieved chunk counts as a _hit_ if it contains that span (after whitespace normalization). Generate candidate questions with an LLM from sampled chunks, then **you review every one** : keep, edit or reject. LLM-written questions tend to copy the chunk’s wording, which flatters keyword search, so rewrite a third of them in your own words.

Nexus Widgets are small battery-powered sensors that measure temperature, humidity and vibration in warehouses, kitchens and workshops. Each widget reports readings every thirty seconds over a low-power radio link to a hub, and the hub forwards the data to the Nexus cloud. This guide explains how to plan a deployment, install and calibrate the hardware, and read the dashboards.

Before ordering hardware, map the spaces you want to monitor. Walk each room and note where the most reliable wall or ceiling mount would sit, how far it is from the nearest hub, and whether metal shelving will block the signal. A widget placed behind a steel rack typically needs a second hub, or a repeater, to keep a steady link. Record the floor plan with rough distances, because the planning tool in the dashboard asks for them later.

Nexus Widgets are battery-powered sensors that report readings to a hub and then to the cloud.

Install the desktop tools and create an account before you pair your first widget.

Power the hub from the included adapter and connect it to the building network with the Ethernet cable. The status light on the hub turns solid green once it has an address and a link to the cloud. A slow blue blink means the hub is waiting for the first widget to join. Pair widgets one at a time by holding the pairing button for three seconds until the widget light flashes white, then bring the widget within one metre of the hub. The pairing completes within about ten seconds, and the widget appears in the device list with its serial number.

Calibration corrects small offsets that come from manufacturing tolerances and from the mounting position. Place a reference thermometer beside a widget and let both settle for fifteen minutes. In the dashboard, open the device page, choose Calibrate, and enter the reference reading. The widget stores the offset and applies it to every later reading. Humidity calibration uses a saturated salt solution in the same way, and the procedure takes about an hour because the sensor needs time to reach equilibrium. Calibrate every widget once after installation and again after any change of mounting position. 

After calibration, check the result on a second reference point. Warm the widget by holding it in a closed hand for two minutes, then compare the reading with a thermometer in a bag beside it. The difference should be under half a degree. If it is larger, repeat the procedure with a fresh reference reading, because a reference that was still warming up is the most common cause of a poor offset. Note the date, the reference used and the final offset in the device logbook so that the history of each widget can be reviewed. 

Sensors drift slowly over several years. A widget that was accurate when installed may read half a degree high after three years, which is inside the stated tolerance but can still matter for cold chain records. Schedule a check every twelve months for devices that hold regulated stock, and recalibrate any widget that falls outside the tolerance printed on its label. Devices that are replaced should be calibrated before they join the hub, so that the new serial number starts with a valid offset.

**Observability.** The ability to understand system behavior from its outputs. Three pillars: **logs** (discrete events), **metrics** (numeric time series such as latency histograms), **traces** (one request’s journey, broken into timed **spans** ). **OpenTelemetry** is the standard vocabulary (trace id, span, attributes). **LLMs are stateless.** Every call must include whatever “memory” you want it to have. Conversation memory is therefore your application’s job: store messages, choose which ones to send, and stay inside the context window. 

|**Strategy**|**How**|**Trade-off**|
|---|---|---|
|Full history|send everything|breaks at length, expensive|
|**Sliding window**|last N messages/tokens|simple, forgets old context|
|Summary buffer|summarize older turns, keep recent verbatim|keeps gist, costs an extra LLM call, can drift|
|Retrieval memory|embed past turns, retrieve relevant ones|powerful, more machinery|

**Server-Sent Events (SSE).** A one-way streaming protocol over plain HTTP: the server keeps the response open and writes events; each event is text lines ending with a blank line: 

event: sources data: {"sources":[{"n":1,"document":"pricing.pdf","section":"Pricing > Enterprise"}]} event: token data: {"t":"Refunds "} event: done data: {"usage":{"input_tokens":1450,"output_tokens":120}} 

Always send **JSON in data:** so newlines and special characters inside tokens can’t corrupt the framing. Compared with WebSockets, SSE is simpler (one direction, auto-reconnect in browsers, works through normal proxies), which is all you need. Send the sources event _first_ so a client can show references before the text arrives. Handle **client disconnects** (stop generating, save what you have) and emit an error event if something fails mid-stream. Disable proxy buffering ( X-Accel-Buffering: no ) or tokens will arrive in one lump.

Learn Claude Code and Retrieval-Augmented Generation by building one serious, resume-grade, backend-only project, with every concept taught at the moment you need it. 

You will build **Nexus RAG** : a multi-tenant document Q&A API with hybrid retrieval, cross-encoder reranking, streaming cited answers, conversation memory, an evaluation harness, tracing, an MCP server, and CI. Retrieval stack runs free on CPU (bge-base + bge-reranker-base 

+ Qdrant + Postgres).

How to Use This Guide

There are no separate “Claude Code lessons” and “RAG lessons”. You build one system, milestone by milestone. When a milestone needs a concept (chunking, JWT, hooks, HNSW, subagents…), the concept is taught right there, together with **why it exists** , the jargon, the design decision, the exact prompts to give Claude Code, and how to verify the result.

Access is controlled by three roles. Viewers can see devices, readings and alerts but cannot change anything. Operators can add and remove widgets, acknowledge alerts and run calibrations. Administrators also manage members, alert channels and the account plan. Assign the smallest role that a person needs, and review the member list every quarter, because people change teams and their access should change with them.

Widget. A battery-powered sensor that measures temperature and humidity and, on some models, vibration. Each widget has a serial number printed on its label and a unique identifier in the dashboard. Widgets never talk to the cloud directly; they always report through a hub. 

Hub. The gateway that joins widgets to the building network and forwards their readings to the cloud. A hub buffers readings during outages, keeps the widget list, and applies firmware updates. Each site needs at least one hub, and large sites may need more than one. 

Calibration offset. A correction value stored on a widget and applied to every reading it produces. Offsets are measured against a reference instrument and remain in place until the widget is calibrated again or removed from the device list.

Can widgets share a hub with other radio equipment? Yes, as long as the other equipment does not use the same channel for long periods. The hub chooses a quiet channel at start-up and moves to another one if interference is detected, which takes about a minute and does not lose any buffered readings.

What happens when the battery of a widget is replaced? The widget keeps its serial number, its calibration offset and its alert rules. Readings resume within one reporting interval once the new battery is seated and the status light has flashed white twice. 

Is there a way to test an alert without waiting for a real event? Yes. Each rule has a Test button that sends a sample notification through the channels attached to that rule. The test notification is marked clearly as a test and does not appear in the event history.
